fields.expected: I'm an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins studying Applied Mathematics & Statistics and Economics, and most of my work has been building machine learning systems that have to hold up in front of real users. At Summer Atlantic Capital / SAC Nexus I build the machine learning core of an anomaly detection and alert prioritization system. I own major parts of the data and ML infrastructure, including the event ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, the public detection API, and the repository and CI scaffold. The modeling work uses temporal sequence models over event streams with RNN and Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, and a learning-to-rank layer, plus a retrieval-augmented LLM layer that turns detections into explanations analysts can act on. The thing I care about there is operational usefulness: a detector that fires too often just creates a second problem, so prioritization, explanation quality, and documented failure modes matter as much as raw accuracy. Earlier, at Intelehealth, I built a resource-availability scoring pipeline in Python across 32 villages and designed an evaluation framework comparing AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard. That work is close to what monitoring and servicing cooling and power equipment seems to require: sensor and event data, prioritized alerts, and a human deciding what to do next.
